item.title: Triangle Covers of Polygons: Approximation Algorithms and Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2610.23634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the geometric set cover problems of covering and partitioning a polygon into a minimum number of triangles. While the decision version of the covering problem is known to be APX-hard and $\exists\mathbb R$-complete (even for polygons without holes and vertices in general position), the computational complexity of partitioning a simple polygon into a minimum number of triangles is open. Our main result refutes a 40 year old conjecture by Asano, Asano, and Pinter stating that the triangle vertices of a minimum partition lie on intersection points of special lines, which are iteratively generated by the polygon vertices and the intersection points. In particular, we show that there exist polygons where all minimum triangle partitions need Steiner points with irrational coordinates. This indicates that the problem might be more complex than previously expected. Complementarily, we provide a simple constant factor approximation to compute a minimum triangle partition of a given polygon (possibly with holes). In the context of coverings, we devise the first constant factor approximation for computing a minimum triangle cover of a simple polygon. For general polygons, an $O(\log n)$-approximation follows by close inspection of previous work.
item.dc:creator: Linda Kleist, Lena Scherzer

item.title: Online geometric matching and segments block points
item.description: arXiv:2610.23130v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given a sequence of online points in general position in the plane, the geometric matching problem asks to match as many points as possible, subject to segment crossing constraints. We initiate the study of online geometric matching with limited crosses. In the $k$-crossing model each matched segment is allowed to have at most $k$ crosses, where $k=0$ corresponds to the online noncrossing matching model for which Bose et al. proved that Greedy is an optimal deterministic algorithm achieving a competitive ratio of $2/3$. In the triangle-free-crossing model no three matched segments are allowed to pairwise cross each other. Interestingly, we show in both cases the performance of Greedy does not improve by allowing crosses, and in fact, becomes worse in the $k$-crossing setting for $k\ge 1$. In the triangle-free-crossing model, we propose a simple two-layer-Greedy deterministic algorithm achieving a competitive ratio $4/5$. More interestingly, we propose and study the underlying segments blocking points extremal problem, and discuss its connection to vertex cover numbers and Ramsey numbers, with interesting open problems that might be of independent interest. We revisit the noncrossing model. We give a randomized algorithm which is an asymmetric version of Kamali et al., improving the competitive ratio from $0.66952$ to $0.67034$. We also show, via a conceptually simple construction, that no randomized algorithm can match more than $6/7$ fraction of points, improving the previous $16/17$ by Boyar et al.
item.dc:creator: Yaqiao Li, Junyi Lin

item.title: Visibility Sets, Empty Pentagons, and Sufficient Conditions for Hexagons
item.description: arXiv:2610.23553v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given a set $S$ of $n$ points in general position in the plane, we define the $C$-set $C(p,q)$ of an oriented edge $(p,q)$ as the set of extreme points of the visibility set $V(p,q)$ facing $(p,q)$. Since every point of $V(p,q)$ that is not in $C(p,q)$ gives rise to an empty convex pentagon having $(p,q)$ as a boundary edge, it is natural to study the properties of $C$-sets in order to bound the number of empty convex pentagons of $S$. We prove tight bounds on the intersection size and union complexity of $C$-sets sharing an endpoint. We also consider the problem of bounding the number of empty pentagons and hexagons in terms of the number of interior and boundary points of $S$. While the hexagon bound is weak, it offers a potential step toward a superlinear lower bound. On the other hand, the two-parameter bound for pentagons, combined with the structural results on $C$-sets, yields a simple proof of an $\Omega(n^{3/2})$ bound for the number of pentagons. While this is a significant improvement over previously published bounds, a recent preprint \cite{Astudillo2026} attains a better bound using completely different methods. Thus, the primary contribution of this paper lies in the structural results about $C$-sets and the two-parameter bounds for empty pentagons and hexagons.
item.dc:creator: Carlos M. Nicolas

item.title: Boundary Detection for High-Dimensional Point Clouds
item.description: arXiv:2610.23590v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce two new methods for boundary detection in high-dimensional point cloud data, intended to work in situations with non-uniform density, high ambient dimension, and substantial noise. Our first method fits a separating hyperplane on local neighborhoods after doing local dimension reduction---this method works best when one can reliably estimate the intrinsic dimension of the data. Our second method measures the directional uniformity of local neighborhoods, and has the best overall performance on synthetic data. In addition to pointwise numerical boundary scores, our algorithms yield an estimated normal vector at each boundary point. We validate our methodology on synthetic data as well as two real examples: we analyze spatial transcriptomics data, where we show that we can detect the boundary of a tumor, and we also study LLM activation geometry.
item.dc:creator: Abigail Hickok, Valerio Galanti, Osama Al Dalahmah, Andrew J. Blumberg

item.title: Puzznic is PSPACE-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2610.23639v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove that deciding solvability of Puzznic, a falling-block puzzle game originally developed by Taito, is PSPACE-complete. To show hardness we construct a self-closing door gadget using Puzznic's game mechanics. For membership, we show that the configuration space is exponentially bounded and apply Savitch's theorem. We also improve an existing NP-completeness proof for a simpler version of the game known as Cubic, showing that this game is NP-complete even when restricted to only two kinds of blocks.
item.dc:creator: Jake Anderson, Lars Magnus Hvattum, Andr\'as Z. Salamon

item.title: Revisiting separators in string graphs, region intersection graphs, and induced-minor-free graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23792v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: String graphs are intersection graphs of continuous curves in the plane. In 2010, Fox and Pach proved that string graphs with $m$ edges admit balanced vertex separators of size $\mathcal{O}(m^{3/4}\sqrt{\log m})$ and conjectured that this bound can be improved to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m})$, which would be optimal. After partial progress, Lee claimed in 2017 to prove this conjecture, and more generally to prove analogous separator theorems for region intersection graphs over minor-closed graph families. A key intermediate step in Lee's approach was a padded decomposition scheme for region intersection graphs. In 2024, Korhonen and Lokshtanov extended Lee's approach to the broader setting of graph classes excluding a fixed graph as an induced minor. These results have since found applications in a wide range of works. Later in 2024, a flaw was discovered in the construction of Lee's padded decomposition scheme, invalidating Lee's as well as Korhonen and Lokshtanov's separator results, and many works relying on them. In this work, we prove that string graphs with $m$ edges admit balanced separators of size $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m})$, and more generally obtain analogous $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m})$ bounds for region intersection graphs over fixed minor-closed graph families and for graphs excluding a fixed graph as an induced minor, thereby repairing the vast majority of the affected works. Furthermore, our balanced separators can be found in polynomial time. Our proof uses a different approach from Lee's and does not rely on padded decompositions. Since padded decompositions have also found applications independent of the separator theorems, particularly for string graphs, we also prove a padded decomposition result for region intersection graphs that is optimal for string graphs. We have formalized both the balanced separator and the padded decomposition results in Lean 4 with mathlib.
item.dc:creator: James Davies, Pawe{\l} Rz\k{a}\.zewski, Jack Spalding-Jamieson, Bartosz Walczak

item.title: Well-quasi-orders on embedded planar graphs
item.description: arXiv:2512.04074v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The central theorem of topological graph theory states that the graph minor relation is a well-quasi-order on graphs. It has far-reaching consequences, in particular in the study of graph structures and the design of (parameterized) algorithms. In this article, we study two embedded versions of classical minor relations from structural graph theory and prove that they are also well-quasi-orders on general or restricted classes of embedded planar graphs. These embedded minor relations appear naturally for intrinsically embedded objects, such as knot diagrams and surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Handling the extra topological constraints of the embeddings requires careful analysis and extensions of classical methods for the more constrained embedded minor relations. We prove that the embedded version of immersion induces a well-quasi-order on bounded carving-width plane graphs by exhibiting particularly well-structured tree-decompositions and leveraging a classical argument on well-quasi-orders on forests. We deduce that the embedded graph minor relation defines a well-quasi-order on plane graphs via their directed medial graphs, when their branch-width is bounded. We conclude that the embedded graph minor relation is a well-quasi-order on all plane graphs, using classical grids theorems in the unbounded branch-width case.
item.dc:creator: Corentin Lunel, Cl\'ement Maria

item.title: Uncovering Hierarchical Structure in LLM Embeddings Using Geometric and Topological Measures
item.description: arXiv:2512.20926v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has driven major advances across scientific domains, yet the hierarchical, geometric, and topological structure of their embedding spaces remains poorly understood. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive framework for evaluating LLM embeddings through six complementary metrics that characterize hierarchy, geometry, and topology. Specifically, $\delta$-hyperbolicity and ultrametricity quantify the degree of tree-like structure, while Neighbor Joining evaluates how well pairwise distances support hierarchical reconstruction. The Ollivier-Ricci curvature captures local geometric behavior, persistent homology measures multiscale topological stability, and fractal dimension estimates intrinsic complexity. Applying this framework to embeddings from multiple protein LLMs, we reveal how different models encode hierarchical relationships and structural organization. Evaluating the structure of these embeddings in the representation space helps improve geometry-aware model design. This is critical in domains such as bioinformatics and healthcare, where real-world hierarchical and relational structures matter. Our results demonstrate that geometric and topological analysis provides a guiding lens for understanding and potentially improving the representational quality of LLM embeddings.
item.dc:creator: Prakash Chourasia, Sarwan Ali, Murray Patterson, Alex Zelikovsky

item.title: Recognizing 2-Layer and Outer $k$-Planar Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2412.04042v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The crossing number of a graph is the least number of crossings over all drawings of the graph in the plane. Computing the crossing number of a given graph is NP-hard, but fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) with respect to the natural parameter. Two well-known variants of the problem are 2-layer crossing minimization and circular crossing minimization, where every vertex must lie on one of two layers, namely two parallel lines, or a circle, respectively. Both variants are NP-hard, but FPT with respect to the natural parameter. Recently, a local version of the crossing number has also received considerable attention. A graph is $k$-planar if it admits a drawing with at most $k$ crossings per edge. In contrast to the crossing number, recognizing $k$-planar graphs is NP-hard even if $k=1$. In this paper, we consider the two above variants in the local setting. The $k$-planar graphs that admit a straight-line drawing with vertices on two layers or on a circle are called 2-layer $k$-planar and outer $k$-planar graphs, respectively. We study the parameterized complexity of the two recognition problems with respect to $k$. For $k=0$, both problems can easily be solved in linear time. Two groups independently showed that outer 1-planar graphs can also be recognized in linear time [Hong et al., Algorithmica 2015; Auer et al., Algorithmica 2016]. One group asked whether outer 2-planar graphs can be recognized in polynomial time. Our main contribution consists of XP-algorithms for recognizing 2-layer $k$-planar graphs and outer $k$-planar graphs. We complement these results by showing that both recognition problems are XNLP-hard. This implies that both problems are W$[t]$-hard for every $t$ and that it is unlikely that they admit FPT-algorithms. On the other hand, we present an FPT-algorithm for recognizing 2-layer $k$-planar graphs where the order of the vertices on one layer is specified.
item.dc:creator: Yasuaki Kobayashi, Yuto Okada, Alexander Wolff
